conclusions: z equals the zero function on I.
|x dot e - 1| <= epsilon; in fact, the displayed components give x dot e=1 exactly.
mathematical_definitions: Let I=Fin 4, identified in construction order with {0,1,2,3}. Vectors are elements of R^4 and matrices are real 4 by 4 matrices.
For vectors p,q, define p dot q=sum_{i in I} p_i q_i and (p componentwise-multiplied by q)_i=p_i q_i. For a matrix M, (Mp)_i=sum_{j in I} M_ij p_j.
Every displayed integer, finite decimal, and scientific literal denotes an exact real rational; no floating-point rounding semantics is present.
translation.proposition_plain_english: This is a closed conjunction about the explicit four-dimensional data above. It asserts that z is the zero vector; that ten specified signed dot products or moment-like expressions have scalar absolute error at most 2/10^15 from the respective targets 1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/6, or 0; and simultaneously that the sum of the componentwise absolute products of x and u=Ae is strictly greater than 1/100.

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: The proposition has no binders, quantifiers, hypotheses, implications, or existential witnesses. Consequently there is no false-premise or missing-witness vacuity; it is a closed numerical conjunction.
All dimensions are fixed at four. The statement gives no result for arbitrary dimensions, matrices, or vectors.
The absolute values in the ten bounds are scalar absolute values. No vector norm or matrix norm occurs.
The final quantity sum_i |x_i||u_i| is not |x dot u|. Thus the proposition explicitly allows cancellation to make |x dot u| at most epsilon while the uncancelled absolute-component sum exceeds 0.01.
The equality z=0 is immediate from the definition of z and contributes no substantive condition on the other data.

The constants are exact real rationals encoded by decimal/scientific notation, so the proposition does not model machine floating-point values, rounding modes, computed-error semantics, or implementation behavior.

The proposition does not assert invertibility, nonsingularity, conditioning, stability, provenance of the data, or any algorithmic relationship beyond the explicitly defined sums, products, and inequalities.
